solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Present journal containing conclusion to report handed down

indicators.note: a conclusion is the end, so only the final letter of the next word is wanted
to contain something is to hold it inside, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: present, as in attending, means here
a diary is a daily journal
the last letter of report

explanation.surface: Someone hands over a current newspaper that carries the end of a story passed down from elsewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' looks like a verb meaning to hand over, but it is the adjective, as in present at a meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Hereditary traits or titles pass from parent to child, which is exactly what being handed down through generations means.

clue.text: Not oddly looking up, you pay the photographer’s agent

indicators.note: leaving out the odd-numbered letters keeps only the even ones, every second letter
in a down clue, looking up means reading from bottom to top, so the order runs backwards

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A client is told they, not the snapper, must settle the bill for the photographer's representative.
explanation.walkthrough: The even letters of 'you pay the' give OPYH, which read upwards becomes the answer. The 'agent' here is chemical, not a person who handles bookings.
explanation.definitionFit: Hypo is the old name for sodium thiosulphate, the fixing chemical used in developing photographs, so a darkroom agent.

clue.text: Bishop hosting a series of bike races has a quiet pedal

indicators.note: a host has guests inside the house, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: RR, Right Reverend, is the title of a bishop
taken as written
the TT, or Tourist Trophy, is the series of motorbike races on the Isle of Man
taken as written
p, piano, is the musical mark for quiet

explanation.surface: A cycling-mad bishop who stages a run of bike races also owns a silent pedal.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue has two separate 'a's and both are used: one sits with the races inside the bishop, the other comes just before quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: A rat-trap pedal is a style of bicycle pedal with toothed metal cages, named for its resemblance to the spring trap.

clue.text: Show lack of tact producing a ring?

definitions.text: Show lack of tact producing a ring?

blocks.note: the straight sense: make an embarrassing social blunder
the literal sense: letting fall something noisy that clangs like a bell as it lands

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for a gaffe is read literally: a clanger is also a thing that clangs, and dropping one would certainly make a ring. 'Ring' is not jewellery.
explanation.definitionFit: The British idiom means making a clumsy, embarrassing remark or mistake, which is a failure of tact in company.

clue.text: Formal attire which restricts work

indicators.note: to restrict is to hem in, so one piece is confined inside another

blocks.note: that and which are interchangeable relative pronouns
an op, short for opus, is a musical work

explanation.surface: Stiff formal clothes that make it hard to do any real work.
explanation.walkthrough: Op, short for opus, is how musicians number a composer's works, so 'work' is a favourite crossword route to those two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall silk hat is worn with morning dress or white tie, so it is an item of formal clothing.

clue.text: Engineers face corrective

blocks.note: REME is the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, a British Army corps
a dial is the face of a clock or watch

explanation.surface: Army engineers are confronted with a punishment meant to put them right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Face' looks like a verb here but is a noun; dial is slang for a person's face as well as a clock's.
explanation.definitionFit: Remedial action or teaching is intended to put right a fault, so it is corrective in purpose.

clue.text: Successive letters daughter’s left for hotel’s cook

indicators.note: something left in favour of another is swapped out, so one letter makes way for a replacement

blocks.note: four consecutive letters of the alphabet
d is the standard abbreviation for daughter
Hotel is the NATO alphabet word for H

explanation.surface: A daughter walks out on the family business to become a hotel's cook.
explanation.walkthrough: In the run CDEF, the D is replaced by H.
explanation.definitionFit: A chef is a professional cook, especially the one in charge of a restaurant or hotel kitchen.

clue.text: Prince’s friend helping briefly with house

indicators.note: said briefly, a word is cut short, losing its final letter

blocks.note: ho is the abbreviation for house
a ration is a portion or helping

explanation.surface: A royal's companion lends a hand for a while around the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Helping' looks like a verb, lending a hand, but it is a noun, a serving of food, and 'briefly' trims its tail.
explanation.definitionFit: Horatio is Hamlet's loyal friend in Shakespeare's play, and Hamlet is the Prince of Denmark.

clue.text: Charge and fine us elderly for misbehaving!

indicators.note: things that misbehave will not stay in line, so these letters are put out of order

blocks.note: f is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An indignant pensioner protests at being billed and penalised for bad behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge' and 'fine' look like money matters, but a charge in heraldry is any device painted on a shield.
explanation.definitionFit: The stylised lily of French royalty is one of the commonest heraldic charges, the emblems borne on a coat of arms.

clue.text: Top up, pre fifty-mile trips here?

indicators.note: to trip is to stumble, so the letters fall into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
L is the Roman numeral for fifty
m is the abbreviation for mile

explanation.surface: Where would you fill your tank before setting out on a fifty-mile journey?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: 'here' points to where you top up before a trip, a nice semi-&lit.
explanation.definitionFit: Motorists fill their fuel tank at a garage dispenser before a long drive, so that is the place meant.

clue.text: Fish for fete’s sandwiches

indicators.note: a sandwich holds its filling between slices, so the letters sit inside the surrounding words

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A fish is on the menu for the sandwiches at the village fete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sandwiches' looks like food but is the verb, holding a word within the words beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The orfe, or ide, is a freshwater fish of the carp family, often golden and kept in ornamental ponds.

clue.text: Stealing from kitty before paying

blocks.note: kitty and pussy are both pet names for a cat
footing the bill is paying it

explanation.surface: Someone helps themselves to the shared fund of money before settling up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stealing' and 'kitty' suggest theft from a cash pool, but stealing here means moving stealthily, and the kitty is a cat.
explanation.definitionFit: Pussyfooting means creeping about cautiously like a cat, which is one sense of stealing, as in stealing across a room.

clue.text: Reliable, cheap accommodation, say, containing study

indicators.note: to contain is to hold inside, so one piece is wrapped around another

blocks.note: B and B, bed and breakfast, is a cheap place to stay
to read a subject is to study it at university
to utter is to say

explanation.surface: Dependable budget lodgings, for instance, that include a room for study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like 'for example', but it is a verb. Bed and breakfast is a guest house offering a room and a morning meal, the classic budget stay in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Bread-and-butter work is the basic, dependable business that keeps you going, so it is steady and reliable.

clue.text: At least three accountants putting book-keeping chap in the picture

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold on to it, so one piece holds another
putting something in is placing it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: CAs, chartered accountants in the plural, plus one more CA
Alan is any man's name
b is the abbreviation for book

explanation.surface: A firm of accountants brings its bookkeeper up to date on what is going on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book-keeping chap' reads as an accountant, but it is a man holding a book. 'In the picture' looks like an idiom for informed, but 'the picture' is a film.
explanation.definitionFit: Casablanca is the 1942 Bogart and Bergman film, and a picture is a common old word for a movie.

clue.text: Is shocking piece of software inadequate too?

indicators.note: something inadequate falls short, so the word comes up one letter short

blocks.note: an app is an application, a piece of software
also and too are synonyms

explanation.surface: A user asks whether a dreadful program is also not up to the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is shocking' is the definition, a verb phrase, not the start of a question; 'shocking' is not describing the software.
explanation.definitionFit: To appal is to horrify or dismay, so something that appals someone is shocking them.

clue.text: Opens act with flourish: a crowning achievement?

indicators.note: a flourish is a showy twirl, so the letters are waved about into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A performer begins the show with a grand gesture, the high point of their career.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opens act' looks like the start of a performance but is only the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A capstone is literally the top stone of a structure, and figuratively the culminating success of a career.

clue.text: A ninth op rectified short passage

indicators.note: to rectify is to put right, so the letters are rearranged into proper order

blocks.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A ninth surgical operation fixed a narrow corridor inside the body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Op' and 'short passage' suggest surgery on a narrow duct, but the passage is liturgical.
explanation.definitionFit: An antiphon is a brief sentence or verse sung before or after a psalm in church services.

clue.text: Performing many functions exhausted yours truly

blocks.note: all in is British slang for worn out
yours truly means me, and one is a formal way to refer to oneself

explanation.surface: A multitasker complains that doing every job has worn them out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yours truly' is the speaker, and 'one' stands for the speaker in formal English.
explanation.definitionFit: An all-in-one device combines several tools in a single unit, like a printer that also scans and copies.

clue.text: Moving easily, finally fulfil one’s part

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the last letter of the word is used

blocks.note: the last letter of fulfil
I is one, and the 's stands for is
some means a part of something

explanation.surface: An actor glides gracefully through the play, at last doing justice to the role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part' suggests a stage role, but it means a portion. 'One's' is read as 'one is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lissome describes a supple, graceful body that bends and moves with ease, like a dancer's.

clue.text: I wish to take off clothes running on island

indicators.note: to clothe is to cover, so one piece is dressed around another

blocks.note: I is the abbreviation for island
to take off is to fly into the air
a machine or show that is running is on

explanation.surface: Someone longs to strip off and jog around a desert island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take off clothes' reads as undressing, but 'take off' is one piece and 'clothes' is the verb, to dress around.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase expresses a longing that things were otherwise, which is the same wishful sense as saying I wish.

clue.text: Zero per cent tax initially after I fail to declare returns

indicators.note: to return is to go back the way you came, so the letters run backwards
initially points to the start, so only the first letter of the word is used
coming after places one piece behind another in the answer

blocks.note: taken as written
in cricket a side that does not declare its innings closed will bat on
the first letter of tax

explanation.surface: A tax return with nothing owed, filed by someone who has left out their income.
explanation.walkthrough: I BAT ON is turned round, and T comes after it. 'Declare' and 'returns' look like tax words, but declaring is closing an innings in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Not a bit means none whatsoever, the same as an amount of zero per cent of anything.

clue.text: Queen visiting for one chance to see old king

indicators.note: a visitor goes into someone else's place, so one piece enters another

blocks.note: eg, for example, means for one
a bet is a chance or gamble
R, for Regina, is the abbreviation for a queen

explanation.surface: A queen drops by, a rare opportunity to meet an ancient monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Regina is Latin for queen, which is why R stands for one, as in ER. 'For one' is the usual crossword way of saying 'for example'.
explanation.definitionFit: Egbert was a ninth-century king of Wessex, often counted as the first ruler of all England.

clue.text: Intelligence facilities incorporated in beds, gates and lamps?

definitions.text: Intelligence facilities incorporated in beds, gates and lamps?

blocks.note: the straight sense: stations set up to eavesdrop on an enemy

blocks.clueFragment: incorporated in beds, gates and lamps?
blocks.note: the playful sense: bedposts, gateposts and lamp-posts are all uprights, imagined here as secretly bugged

explanation.surface: Spy agencies have hidden their bugs in bedsteads, garden gates and street lights.
explanation.walkthrough: Beds, gates and lamps all have posts, so the question imagines those posts eavesdropping; 'intelligence' means spying, not cleverness.
explanation.definitionFit: Military and security services use forward stations to monitor enemy communications and gather information by overhearing.

clue.text: Female rivals at table with the papers?

blocks.note: at bridge, East and North sit on opposing sides
ID papers are identity documents

explanation.surface: Women competing at the breakfast table while reading the morning newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Papers' suggests newspapers, but it is identity papers. In bridge North-South play against East-West, so E and N are opponents.
explanation.definitionFit: Enid is a woman's name, and crosswords routinely define a given name by the sex of its usual bearer.

clue.text: Men to go back, always ending in retreat

indicators.note: taking every word's end means only the final letter of each is kept

blocks.note: the final letters of these four words

explanation.surface: Soldiers are ordered to fall back, as they always do at the end of a retreat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Always' means every time, so the ending is taken from each word in turn. 'Go back' tempts you to reverse something; nothing reverses.
explanation.definitionFit: A nook is a sheltered corner or secluded spot where one can withdraw, so it serves as a retreat.

clue.text: Thrilled reaction at lazy morning touring second rate dump

indicators.note: to tour a place is to travel around it, so one piece goes round another

blocks.note: whee is a cry of delight
a lie-in is a morning spent lazing in bed
B is the grade for second rate, below A

explanation.surface: Someone thrilled by a lie-in is taken to see a shabby tip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dump' looks like a shabby place, but here it is a household container for rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: A wheelie bin is the large wheeled rubbish bin British households put out for collection, a place to dump waste.

clue.text: Take off, and cross summit

blocks.note: to ape someone is to take them off, to mimic them
an X is a cross

explanation.surface: A climber sets off and crosses the peak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take off' suggests departing, but it is the British sense of imitating someone.
explanation.definitionFit: The apex is the highest point of something, the tip of a mountain or triangle, synonymous with its top.

clue.text: Started with a ten-digit sum, originally, that’s spent

indicators.note: originally points to the origin, the start, so only the first letter is wanted
something spent is used up and broken, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
the first letter of sum

explanation.surface: A huge ten-figure sum was started and has already been spent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spent' looks like money going out, but it signals a rearrangement of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To instigate something is to set it in motion or bring it about, so instigated means began or started.
